narrative.text: Describes how digital technologies are shaping global health, citing the 2030 Agenda and UN reviews of the World Summit on the Information Society. It argues that digital and frontier technologies can help reach WHO's triple billion targets and improve diagnosis, treatment and self-care. It notes that many countries still need support for national strategies and that digital health should be ethical, safe, equitable and interoperable.

Sets out the strategy's vision of better health for everyone through appropriate, affordable and sustainable person-centred digital health solutions, including for epidemics and pandemics. It lists the conditions under which digital health will be valued and calls for evidence on global solutions in different country contexts.

States the strategy's purpose of strengthening health systems by applying digital technologies for patients, professionals, providers and industry, and defines digital health broadly to include eHealth and emerging fields. It stresses health data protection, interoperability and appropriate sharing of data for public benefit. It ends by saying the strategy will produce concrete actions and results between 2020 and 2025.
States the guiding principle that each country owns its digital health action plan and will adopt digital health in line with its own context and resources.

Explains that digital health initiatives need an integrated, costed strategy with strong governance, standards and architecture. It warns that poorly coordinated initiatives lead to fragmented stand-alone systems.
A heading fragment introducing the four guiding principles.

Presents the principle of appropriate use of digital technologies as digital public goods, with protection from misinformation, cyber threats and misuse of health data. It notes the importance of digital determinants of health and lists qualities that appropriate digital health should have, including managing digital waste.
States the principle that investment is urgently needed to overcome barriers faced by least-developed countries, such as infrastructure, skills, finance, connectivity and standards.

Introduces strategic objective 1 on global collaboration and knowledge transfer, aiming to align countries and stakeholders on shared opportunities and risks. It covers maximizing partnerships and assessing new health technologies with norms and standards.

Introduces the four strategic objectives and lists policy options for objective 1, such as co-creating the strategy and knowledge management. It begins the expected outputs, including governance mechanisms and regular multistakeholder groups.

Describes strategic objective 2 on helping each country own and strengthen a national digital health strategy, with core components from leadership and investment to standards and interoperability. It lists policy options such as stakeholder engagement, a national roadmap, open data standards and legal and ethical frameworks for patient safety and data security.

Describes strategic objective 3 on strengthening digital health governance and capacity, with standards for security, privacy, interoperability and ethical data use and a research agenda. It lists policy options and outputs such as a health data regulatory framework and voluntary interoperability guidance. It ends with guidance on digital hospitals and recommendations on pseudonymizing and anonymizing health data.

Describes strategic objective 4 on people-centred health systems enabled by digital health, covering digital literacy, gender equality and readiness of health workers. It lists policy options on population health management, public participation and training. Outputs include global minimum health data standards and guidance on personalized medicine.
Describes the commit component of the framework for action, asking countries and stakeholders to make voluntary commitments to implement the strategy.
Describes the catalyse component, creating a cooperative environment for scaling up digital health technologies, with the Secretariat promoting collaboration.
Explains that the framework for action provides structure and tools for collaboration, guided by four components and accompanied by an action plan for each strategic objective.
Describes the measure component, under which the Secretariat will assess the strategy's effectiveness from global data and report to Member States.
Describes the enhance and iterate component, with annual review of the action plan to decide on new cycles of action. It also notes collaboration on quality-assured digital global public goods.
Introduces implementation of the strategy and action plan in line with country health priorities, universal health coverage and WHO's Thirteenth General Programme of Work, with a summary figure.

Sets out general principles for implementing the strategy with Member States and many stakeholders, with timelines, milestones and core process indicators. It discusses financing needs and stresses that countries should choose actions suited to their digital health maturity. It notes that the annex describes short-, medium- and long-term actions and that progress will be reported to the Assembly.

Sets out specific principles for a national interoperable digital health ecosystem based on agreed use cases, standards and a sound legal framework. It covers protecting health data, digital identification and a coordinated approach to the economics of health data.

Describes monitoring and evaluation through standard metrics on digital health maturity and a value measurement model, while minimizing extra data burdens. Based on the shown end, the block also begins the glossary with definitions such as digital divide and digital health.

The glossary of the digital health strategy, defining terms such as artificial intelligence, big data, blockchain, digital health, infodemic, interoperability and telemedicine, with source notes. It is followed by the annex setting out proposed actions for Member States, the Secretariat and partners. The annex is organized by the four strategic objectives and by short-, medium- and long-term time frames. The end lists actions under objective 4 on people-centred health systems, such as supporting interoperable digital systems to improve quality, coverage and access.

The front matter of the Global strategy on digital health 2020–2025 (WHO, 2021), with ISBNs, licence terms and the table of contents. It includes acknowledgements describing the two-year consultation that led to adoption by the Seventy-third World Health Assembly. Based on the shown end, it also contains the introduction tracing the strategy to earlier eHealth and digital health resolutions, with notes citing sources such as the WHO–ITU National eHealth Strategy Toolkit.
